title: CV engineer — detection and decision
you_are: You own the decision. A camera watches a site entrance, and you are the one who decides whether the person walking through it is wearing a helmet — and whether that is worth interrupting somebody over.
stakes: Both directions of being wrong cost something real. Miss a bare head and you have a safety incident nobody was warned about. Alert on a compliant worker often enough and the site supervisor mutes the system, at which point you have built nothing.
deliverable: check_frame(frame) → zero or more alerts, one per person who is in frame and not wearing a helmet.

concept.question: Your system alerts on workers without helmets. What has to be true before the alert can be raised, and why would building the alert first still look like it works?
concept.answer: An alert is a claim about a condition, so the condition has to be established before the alert exists — otherwise the alert is really firing on the last thing you did evaluate, which here is just "a person is in frame". It looks correct for as long as everyone in your test footage happens to be non-compliant, and the first compliant worker is the first time you find out.
concept.transfers_to: Anything that acts on a predicate you have not computed yet: authorising before checking a permission, retrying before classifying the error, sending a notification before confirming the state change it describes.

lesson.title: An alert is a claim about a condition

panels.title: Two things have to work. Only one of them is visible
panels.body: The system watches a feed and raises an alert when someone is working without a helmet. That needs something to decide whether a helmet is present, and something to raise the alert. The alert is the part you can demo.

items: decide whether the helmet is there

panels.title: Choose, and then read on
panels.body: Pick the order you would build in. The second option is the one most people actually do, because a person detector is already in the box and a helmet classifier is a week of work.

choices.label: Detect the helmet first — alert on what the detector says
Wire the alert on the person detector now, add the helmet check after

panels.title: Your test footage, and a compliant shift
panels.body: Same site, same camera, two days.

cases.input: The test footage you recorded — nobody on it is wearing a helmet
A shift where the crew is compliant and every worker has a helmet on

results.alert_first: an alert for every worker on site

panels.note: Built the second way, the alert is not firing on "no helmet". It is firing on "a person is in frame" — the last thing you actually evaluated. Your test footage could never have told you, because on that footage those two are the same set.

panels.title: Where have you seen this shape before?
panels.body: Take the camera out of it. Something acted on a condition, and the thing that establishes that condition was not built yet.
panels.prompt: Before you open the flashcard: name two other places in your code that act on a predicate nothing has computed yet. For each, work out what the code is *actually* keying on instead.

owns.intent: Find the people in the frame. No people, no decision to make.
owns.why_yours: Every downstream decision is per-person, so the set of people is the input to all of them.

owns.intent: For each person found, decide whether they are wearing a helmet — and admit when the answer is uncertain.
owns.why_yours: This is the actual judgement the system exists to make. It cannot be delegated to a threshold somebody else owns.

owns.intent: Raise one alert per person who is in frame and established as not wearing a helmet.
owns.why_yours: The alert is only as trustworthy as the check behind it, so whoever owns the check owns the alert.

given.contract: Hands you decoded frames as BGR arrays at 5fps. Frames may be dropped; they are never out of order.
Accepts an alert and stores it durably. It will not deduplicate for you.

acceptance.given: a worker wearing a helmet walks through frame
a worker with no helmet walks through frame
